intro: A child announces something momentous, in a mock-ceremonial A major. The second section is marked ff and repeated; then the opening comes back.
question: How does a piece sound serious and amused at once?

sections.label: B · ff, played twice
sections.mNote: eight bars repeated; the repeat is taken

cues.title: Accented chords, octave basses
cues.text: Three beats to the bar in A major, marked f. Nearly every chord carries an accent, and the left hand plays octaves. The effect is a small procession with a straight face, which is the joke of the title.
cues.evidence: First edition p. 10 (IMSLP #03060): 3/4, three sharps, f at the opening, accent marks on most chords, left-hand octaves. Report: A major (global r = 0.88), −13.4 dB at 0:00 rising to −8.8 dB by 0:15.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: ff, then the same eight bars again
cues.text: The second section is marked ff and enclosed in repeat signs. This performance takes the repeat: the form analysis finds the same music at about 0:15–0:26 and 0:29–0:39, thirteen seconds apart.
cues.evidence: Report: novelty 0.82 at 0:14. Form analysis: 0:15.5–0:26 matches 0:28.5–0:39 (lag 13 s, mean 0.97, the closest recurrence in this piece). Score p. 10: ff at the opening repeat sign of the second section and a closing repeat sign.

cues.title: A critic counts the hands
cues.text: Ludwig Rellstab reviewed the set in 1839 and judged it unplayable for the children he supposed it was for, since a child would need three hands. Schumann told Heinrich Dorn he had rarely met anything so clumsy and narrow-minded as that review.
cues.evidence: Zwickau catalogue, item 11: Rellstab, Iris im Gebiete der Tonkunst, 1839, “ein Kind das nicht drei Hände hat”. Schumann to Heinrich Dorn, 1839: “Ungeschickteres und Bornierteres ist mir aber nicht leicht vorgekommen”, quoted in GMTH Proceedings 2006 (article 117), which cites Edler 1982; schumann-portal.de/3213.html quotes the next sentences of the same letter.

transitions.title: Forte gives way to ff
transitions.how: After the opening eight bars the second section begins at a repeat sign and the mark is raised to ff. The accented chords now sit above falling left-hand figures and the harmony turns towards D major, the subdominant, so the procession is louder and more energetic. The metre is that of the opening; the contrast is one of weight, texture and key region.
transitions.evidence: Report: novelty 0.82 at 0:14; level −8.8 dB at 0:15 and −7.2 dB at 0:20; local key D major from 0:15 to 0:35 (r = 0.82–0.89), A major again at 0:40. Mutopia transcription (SchumannOp15No06.ly) shows D-major chords and a G natural in the middle section. Score p. 10: ff at the repeat sign that begins the second section; falling left-hand figures in the third system.

transitions.title: The repeat ends and the opening returns
transitions.how: The closing repeat sign sends the music back through the ff section once; after its second pass the opening march returns, marked f as at the start, and the piece closes on the music it began with.
transitions.evidence: Report: novelty 1.00 at 0:40 and 0.68 at 0:46; level −11.2 dB at 0:40. Score p. 10, fourth system: closing repeat sign followed by f and the opening music.

facts: Piano with Friedrich Wieck; composition with Heinrich Dorn; extensive private study of Bach and Beethoven
Co-founder of the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik, 1834; editor until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
Leipzig Conservatoire teacher; municipal music director, Düsseldorf, 1850–53
composer.background:
Schumann grew up in Zwickau, where his father August was a bookseller and publisher. Reading and music developed together: Jean Paul’s novels, with their interruptions, doubles and changes of narrative voice, mattered alongside piano lessons. Sent to Leipzig to study law in 1828, he spent more time on music and literature; a period in Heidelberg did not reconcile him to a legal career. He returned to Leipzig to study piano seriously with Friedrich Wieck. Wieck’s daughter Clara, already performing publicly as a child, gave him an immediate example of the professional discipline he hoped to acquire.

A persistent problem with his right hand ended the prospect of a virtuoso career. The familiar account of a finger-strengthening device leaves the injury’s medical cause uncertain. Composition and criticism became his principal occupations. The early published piano works already had distinct literary and formal premises: the Abegg Variations derive a theme from letters, while Papillons relates its dances to the masked-ball ending of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre. The miniatures’ sudden juxtapositions recreate the experience of a narrative changing speakers and levels.
composer.epithet: His music lets remembered fragments, concealed names and competing inner voices interrupt the forms that contain them.
